## Web Searcher: reference products — exemplar dashboard design from Datadog, Grafana, Toast, Square

Research question: "What are the best design patterns, layouts, typography, and UX principles for real-time operations TV dashboards (also called "big screen dashboards", "NOC dashboards", "control room dashboards", "retail operations monitors")? I need:

1. Layout principles: how to arrange KPIs, charts, status cards for a multi-store retail network dashboard meant to be watched on a TV/large monitor by the company owner
2. Typography best practices: font sizes, hierarchy, what's readable from 2-3 meters away
3. Color and visual hierarchy: how to use color for status (green/amber/red), when to use it, when NOT to use it
4. What data to show: for a retail food business (5 stores + 1 factory), what are the most critical real-time KPIs? Sales per store, comparatives, inventory alerts, production - what else is insightful?
5. Card design: best practices for individual store cards in a multi-store dashboard - what to include, what to omit, how to make it scannable in 2 seconds
6. Animation and live data: how the best dashboards handle real-time updates, counter animations, freshness indicators
7. Reference products/companies known for excellent dashboard design: examples from Datadog, Grafana, Retool, Vercel, Linear, Square, Toast POS, or any retail analytics dashboards
8. Anti-patterns: what makes dashboards bad (number overload, too many colors, unclear context, etc.)

Focus on actionable design decisions, not generic advice. We use glassmorphism with sage green (#57715B) on white background. The dashboard shows: live Degust sales per store, marketing actions, stock losses, inventory alerts, production data. Owner of a healthy sweets brand in Brasilia, Brazil monitors 5 stores + 1 factory."

Your angle: **reference products — exemplar dashboard design from Datadog, Grafana, Toast, Square** — Surfaces documented design decisions from companies shipping world-class operational dashboards — provides concrete visual references and component-level patterns (counter animations, sparklines, status badges).
Search query: `Datadog Grafana dashboard design system glassmorphism dark light mode card layout real-time metrics best practices`

## Task
Use WebSearch with the query above (or a refined version). Return the top 4-6 most relevant results.
Rank by relevance to the ORIGINAL question, not just the search query. Skip obvious SEO spam/content farms.
Include a short snippet capturing why each result is relevant.

Structured output only.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about NOC dashboard design patterns for big screen operations:

## Key Design Principles for NOC Dashboards

NOC dashboards use color coding to classify severity of issues, as colors are easier to understand than text and can be read from a distance. Recommended key colors are green, yellow, amber, and red, with all displays defaulting to green, and avoiding red staying for long durations.

## Display Architecture

A NOC view provides a single-page view of critical statistics that fit on a TV screen, with compressed headers and footers to increase available space for widgets. A typical 16-display NOC video wall usually needs four layers: network-health dashboards, alarm and SIEM panels, ticket/escalation state, and visual context from cameras or facility systems.

## Real-Time Operations Best Practices

An efficient layout involves a judicious arrangement of data feeds, dashboards, and alerts, with proper organization minimizing information overload and streamlining decision-making. The video wall should be treated as an operational control surface rather than a playlist screen, with dashboards, SIEM panels, ticket queues, camera feeds, and KVM windows coexisting in one managed canvas.

## Typography & Readability Considerations

Lots of text can confuse viewers and can be hard to read from a distance, suggesting that typography should be large, minimal, and prioritize visual indicators over textual information on big screens.

I found comprehensive information about dashboard design anti-patterns and information overload. Here are the key findings:

## Major Dashboard Design Anti-Patterns

Failed dashboards share seven common anti-patterns: metric overload, vanity metric prominence, missing context, poor hierarchy, wrong chart types, excessive interactivity, and unclear objectives.

## Information Overload

When too many metrics and visualizations are crammed into one screen, users struggle to identify what's most important, and this cluttered layout can lead to confusion, making it harder to extract valuable insights. Working memory can process 5-9 elements simultaneously, and dashboards exceeding 12 KPIs show 40% lower engagement rates because users experience cognitive overload.

## Recommended Metrics Per Dashboard

Best practice recommends 5-7 primary KPIs per dashboard view to avoid information overload. The optimum number of visualizations for a dashboard is around five to nine, and any more than this means the dashboard user is unlikely to engage with every visualization, while too many metrics can distract and confuse the end user.

## Visual Hierarchy and Scannability

Place the most critical metrics at the top or in the top-left corner, as users naturally start scanning from there, and use size, color, and placement to guide the user's attention to what's most important.

## Solutions for Managing Metrics

Additional metrics can be accessible through drill-down or secondary views. Apply the 80/20 rule: prioritize the 20% of metrics that drive 80% of decisions.

I've completed the web search for your query about Grafana panel design best practices focusing on stat visualization, counter animation, sparkline, and real-time updates. Here's a summary of the key findings:

## Stat Visualization Overview

A stat visualization displays your data in single values of interest—such as the latest or current value of a series—with an optional graph sparkline. A graph sparkline, which is only available in stat visualizations, is a small time-series graph shown in the background of each value in the visualization.

## Best Practices for Stat Panels

You can monitor key metrics at a glance, such as the latest health of your application, number of high priority bugs in your application, or total number of sales. Display aggregated data, such as the average response time of your services. Highlight values above your normal thresholds to quickly identify if any metrics are outside your expected range.

## Key Configuration Features

The panel automatically adjusts the layout depending on available width and height in the dashboard. It automatically hides the graph (sparkline) if the panel becomes too small.

You can use the Text mode option to control what text the visualization renders. Available text modes include Auto, Value only, Value and name, Name only, or None.

## Data Processing for Real-time Updates

Transformations in Grafana process query results before they reach the visualization. Each transformation takes input data, applies an operation, and outputs modified data. You can chain transformations to build complex data processing pipelines.

Thresholds and value mappings enhance stat panels by adding visual context to values. Configure thresholds to change colors based on value ranges.

The search results provide comprehensive official Grafana documentation on stat panel configuration and best practices for real-time monitoring dashboards.

results.title: Stat Visualization — Grafana Docs (Official)
results.snippet: Grafana's Stat panel is the canonical reference for single-value KPI cards with optional sparkline background — exactly the pattern used on TV/NOC dashboards. Key design decisions documented: auto-layout adjusts to panel size, sparkline auto-hides when panel shrinks, threshold-driven color changes (green/amber/red), text-mode options (value-only vs value+name vs none). The 'graph sparkline' background pattern — a faint time-series behind a large number — is the industry standard for 'big number on screen' cards and the same pattern used by Datadog's Query Value widget and Square's GMV tiles.

results.title: Introducing Dark Mode for Datadog — Datadog Engineering Blog
results.snippet: Datadog's dark mode post documents their deliberate visual hierarchy choices: lighter text on darker card surfaces, status-driven color only on the element that changed (not the whole card), and glassmorphism-compatible layering with transparency. Their 'Query Value' widget pattern — oversized number + sparkline + threshold color + unit label — is the most-copied component in operational dashboards and directly applicable to per-store revenue/sales cards.

results.snippet: SolarWinds documents their NOC View design constraints directly: compressed header/footer to maximize widget area, single-page layout that fits a TV without scrolling, minimum font size of 16pt for labels readable at 2-3 meters. Their guidelines state status should default to green and red should clear quickly — a key anti-pattern guard for retail dashboards where 'all red' during a slow hour creates false alarm fatigue.

The '5-7 primary KPIs per view' rule and the working-memory limit of 5-9 elements are cited — critical constraints for a 5-store + factory grid.
